title: No sea days, and no day off
subtitle: A river week gives you a new town most mornings. That is a pace, not a rest.

text: A river cruise has no day where nothing is expected of you.
sub: Ocean itineraries build in sea days on purpose — the spa, a long lunch, a book. On a river the ship arrives somewhere every morning and there is always something worth walking to.

points.label: Ocean, day three
points.value: A sea day. Nothing scheduled, and that emptiness is the entire point of it.

points.label: River, day three
points.value: A new town by breakfast, a guided morning, and the ship moves again before dinner.

points.label: By day six
points.value: Six towns behind you. Wonderful, and more tiring than the brochure suggests.

points.label: The fix
points.value: Skip one excursion on purpose. The sundeck between locks is the sea day you didn't get.

items.head: Anyone recovering
items.body: A week with no built-in rest day is the wrong week after surgery, or after a hard year.

items.head: Slow risers
items.body: Guided mornings start early, because the ship has to sail again in the afternoon.

items.head: Sea-day loyalists
items.body: If your best cruise memory is a lounger and a novel, ocean is quietly the right answer.

left.label: River week
items: No day with nothing in it

right.label: Ocean week
items: Sea days built into the route

text: No sea days is the best argument for a river, and against it.
sub: It is why you see so much in seven nights. It is also why some travellers come home needing a holiday. Know which of those you are before you book.

title: Save this if you're choosing between the two
body: Or send me the week you have in mind and I'll mark the day I'd protect as your own.
